hnfm: Building a Local-First AI Podcast Generator for Hacker News

hnfm is my hackathon project for the OpenAI Open Model Hackathon. It's an application that takes Hacker News articles and automatically transforms them into podcast-style videos using a full suite of AI models.

Once I proved the concept worked, I gutted the initial code and rebuilt with a stronger spec:
Wrapped WhisperX and DIA in FastAPI servers for reliable inference.
Added endpoints for managing VRAM by unloading TTS models between runs.
Split long-running jobs into queued tasks.
Centralized Redis client logic to avoid duplication across tasks.

: Encoding best practices into coding agents prevented regressions and kept the codebase clean.

There are several other projects attempting to generate automated podcasts from Hacker News. Google's NotebookLM popularized the idea of creating podcasts of your documents, but it is not open source. NVIDIA has an open-source Blueprint called "pdf-to-podcast" that was a helpful reference, but it uses Eleven Labs for audio generation.
The AI podcast generation landscape offers several distinct approaches:
Podcastfy.ai - Open-source Python tool for multi-modal content (websites, PDFs, videos) to multilingual audio conversations
TwoCast - One-click 3-5 minute two-person podcast generator with multiple TTS platform support
Hackercast - Scrapes and summarizes Hacker Newsletter content using Langchain/GPT-4
Hacker News Recap - Daily AI-generated recaps of top HN posts
Hacker News 每日播报 - Chinese-language daily HN summaries with Edge TTS
Personalized News Generator - Custom podcasts based on user interests and news using Gemini/ElevenLabs

AutoPod - Converts reading lists to podcasts via n8n workflows (as low as $0.20/20min)
Video Content:
HN to Video Content - n8n workflow converting HN articles to videos using AI image/video generation

There are some amazing options for doing local generative video. Wan 2.2 is one such model. This would be interesting to explore, but I decided not to include any video generation in this project. Video generation takes a lot of time compared to image generation and TTS.

For me, hnfm represents a "prosumer" approach to AI - consuming content from Hacker News, but also producing something new with it. It's commentary, transformation, and reimagining, all in one.

I've made the project open source because I believe experiments like this should be shared. The closed-source AI ecosystem is growing rapidly, but it's vital that we also push forward what's possible with
running on personal hardware. It's not just about cost or performance - it's about ownership, freedom, and creative expression.
Building hnfm was challenging, rewarding, and a lot of fun. It's a small glimpse into what's possible with state-of-the-art open source AI running on consumer hardware.

I made hnfm with AI assisted coding, but I think it would be interesting to try to replicate this project with n8n, a low-code/no-code workflow tool that is very popular for AI-powered content creation.

Every one of these still runs at home. Nothing calls a paid API.
It grew a memory and an opinion
Stories, runs and segments moved from Redis to Postgres, and every step of every run is recorded with its inputs, so any step can be looked at and run again.
Each new story is scored for how interesting it is and how well it can be produced. Most of what reaches Hacker News never becomes anything.
For the stories worth making, a brief is written first: the thesis, the facts, the numbers, what the comment thread added, and what the source does not establish.
The same briefs feed a written digest that is sent to an e-reader each morning.

The single PC became a small home cluster. hn.fm is packaged as a Helm chart. A push to the git server builds the images, and a deploy controller rolls them out. Media lives in an S3-compatible object store. The "one RTX 4090" in the section above is now several machines, each serving one model.

The newest part is an internet radio station. It runs six shows a day, each with two hosts and its own music, and it is made of segments: headlines, a two-host conversation about one story, a phone-in where callers voice points from the comment thread, a bulletin at the top of the hour, the front page read as a weather forecast, and one short song an hour about a story.
Three decisions make it work on a small local model.
Code decides the shape of the hour. The model decides what goes in it.
An earlier version asked the model to plan thirty minutes of radio and then repaired the plan. Now the model is asked one question per block: which story goes in which slot.
Pieces are written from a fact sheet and a worked example.
The model follows an example far more reliably than a rule, and it repeats whatever it is shown, so it is shown only a short list of checked facts.
Every spoken line is listened to before it airs.
The speech recogniser transcribes it and the transcript is compared with the script. A line that came out wrong is spoken again.
The station only makes new programming while someone is listening. The rest of the time it plays music it has already made.

The "Generative Video" section above said video generation was left out because it was slow. That is still the state of things: the video model exists on the cluster and is not yet part of the station.
